source_text: Sed quoniam nos sermo commonuit de iudicio futuro et de retributione ac suppliciis peecatorum, secundum quod comminantur sanctae scripturae et ecclesiastica praedicatio continet, eo quod iudiei tempore ‘ignis aeternus- et -tenebrae exteriores- et “carcer- et -caminus- et alia his similia peccatoribus praeparata sint, videamus quid etiam de his sentiri. oporteat, Sed ut ad haec competenti ordine veniatur, prius mihi videtur de resurrectione sermo movendus, ut sciamus quid est illud quod vel ad supplieium vel ad requiem ac beatitudinem veniet; de quo et in aliis quidem libris, quos de resurrectione scripsimus, plenius disputavimus et quid nobis de hoc videretur ostendimus. Sed et nune propter consequentiam tractatus pauca inde repetere non videtur absurdum, maxime propter hoe quod offenduntur quidam in ecclesiastica fide, quod velut stulte et penitus insipienter de resurrectione credamus, praecipue haeretici, quibus hoc modo arbitror respondendum. Si confitentur etiam ipsi quia resurrectio sit mortuorum, respondeant nobis: quid est quod mortuum est, nonne corpus? Corporis ergo resurrectio fiet. Tum deinde dicant si utendum putant nobis esse corporibus aut non? Arbitror apostolo Paulo dicente quia “seminatur corpus animale, resurget corpus spiritale”, istos negare non posse quod ‘corpus resurgat vel quia in resurrectione corporibus utamur. Quid ergo? Si certum est quia corporibus nobis utendum sit, et ‘corpora’ ea, quae ceciderunt, ‘resurgere’ praedicantur (non enim proprie resurgere dicitur nisi id, quod ante ceciderit), null dubium est idcirco ea ‘resurgeres, ut his iterum ex resurrectione induamur. Alterum ergo haeret ex altero. Nam et si resurgunt corpora, sine dubio ad indumentum nostri resurgunt, et si necesse est nos esse in corporibus (sieut certe necesse est), non in alüs quam in nostris corporibus esse debemus. Quae si verum est quod resurgunt et :spiritaha- resurgunt, dubium non est quin abiecta corruptione et deposita mortalitate resurgere dicantur a mortuis; ahoquin vanum videbitur et superfluum resurgere quem a mortuis, ut iterum moriatur. Quod ita demum intellegi evidentius potest, si qui diligenter advertat, quae sit -animalis corporis- qualitas, quae in terram seminata ‘spiritalis corporis. reparet qualitatem. Ex -animali- namque “corpore- ipsa virtus resurrectionis et gratia ‘spiritale corpus’ educit, cum id ab -indigmitate- transmutat ad ‘gloriam”. 2. Quoniam ergo haeretici eruditissimi sibi videntur et sapientissimi, interrogabimus eos, si omne corpus schema aliquod habet, id est aliquo habitu deformetur. Et si quidem dixerint esse corpus quod non aliquo habitu deformetur, imperitissimi omnium atque insipientissimi videbuntur. Nullus enim hoc negabit, nisi sit ab omni eruditione penitus alienus. Si vero secundum id, quod consequens est, dixerint quia omne corpus certo quo habitu deformatur, requiremus ab eis, si possunt nobis ‘spiritalis corporis’ habitum demonstrare atque deseribere; quod utique facere nullo modo poterunt. Sed et differentias eorum, qui resurgunt, inquiremus ab eis. Quomodo ostendent verum esse illud, quod dietum est quia “ala caro volucrum, alia piscium; et corpora caelestia et corpora terrestria; sed alia quidem caelestium gloria, alia vero terrestrium, alia gloria solis, alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarum, stella enim ab stella differt in gloria; ita et resurrectio mortuorum”? Secundum istam ergo consequentiam caelestium corporum ostendant nobis differentias gloriae eorum qui resurgunt, et si ullo genere conati fuerint secundum caelestium corporum differentias aliquam excogitare rationem, quaeremus ab eis, ut etiam secundum terrenorum corporum comparationem differentias resurreetionis adsignent. Nos vero ita intellegimus, quod volens apostolus describere, quanta esset differentia eorum, qui resurgent “in gloria, id est sanctorum, comparationem caelestium corporum sumpsit dicens: “Alia gloria solis, alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarume. Et iterum volens differentias eorum docere, qui in hae vita non expurgati ad resurrectionem venient, id est peccatores, de terrenis sumit exemplum dicens: “Alia caro volucrum, alia piscium”. Digne etenim sanctis caelestia, terrena peccatoribus comparantur. Haee quidem dicta sint adversum eos, qui “resurrectionem mortuorume, id est resurrectionem corporum negant. 3. Nune vero sermonem convertimus ad nonnullos nostrorum, qui vel pro intelleetus exiguitate vel explanationis inopia valde vilem et abiectum sensum de resurrectione corporis introducunt. (Quos interrogamus, quomodo intellegant ‘animale corpus- gratia resurrectionis immutandum et “spiritale- futurum, et quomodo quod ‘in infirmitate seminatur-. resurrecturum sentiant ‘in virtutes, et quod ‘in ignobilitate-, quomodo -resurgat in gloria; et quod ‘in eorruptione., quomodo ad “neorruptionem- transferatur. Quod utique si credunt apostolo quia corpus ‘in gloria et in virtute et in incorruptibilitate- resurgens, ‘spiritale” iam effectum sit, absurdum videtur et contra apostoli sensum dicere, id rursum ‘carnis et sanguinis- passionibus implicari, cum manifeste dieat apostolus: “Quoniam caro et sanguis regnum dei non possidebunt, neque corruptio incorruptionem possidebit”, Sed et illud quomodo aecipiunt, quod dicit apostolus quia “omnes autem immutabimur”? Quae utique immutatio secundum illum ordinem, quem superius diximus, expectanda est, in qua sine dubio dignum aliquid divina gratia sperare nos convenit; quod futurum credimus hoc ordine quo “nudum granum frumenti aut alicuius ceterorum” in terra seminatum describit apostolus, eui “deus dat corpus prout voluit”, cum prius "granum- ipsum “frumenti- -mortuum fuerit. Ita namque etiam nostra corpora velut “granum- cadere in terram putanda sunt; quibus insita ratio ea, quae substantiam continet corporalem, quamvis emortua fuerint corpora et corrupta atque dispersa, verbo tamen dei ratio illa ipsa, quae semper in substantia corporis salva est, erigat ea de terra et restituat ac reparet, sicut ea virtus, quae inest in grano frumenti, post corruptionem eius ac mortem reparat ac restituit granum in culmi corpus et spicae.- Et ita his quidem, qui regni eaelorum hereditatem consequi merebuntur, ratio illa reparandi corporis, quam supra diximus, dei iussu ex terreno et ‘animali corpore- “corpus- reparat ‘spiritale”, quod habitare possit in caelis; his vero, qui inferioris meriti fuerint vel abiectioris aut etiam ultimi et abstrusi, pro uniuscuiusque vitae atque animae dignitate etiam gloria corporis et dignitas dabitur: ita tamen ut etiam eorum, qui ad ‘ignem aeternum- vel ad ‘supplieia” destinandi sunt, per ipsam resurrectionis permutationem ita corpus incorruptum sit quod resurgit, ut ne suppliciis quidem corrumpi valeat ae dissolvi. 4. Si ergo ita se habet qualitas eius corporis, quod resurget a mortuis, videamus nunc quid sibi velit ‘ignis aeterni- comminatio. 4. Invenimus namque in Esaia propheta designari uniuscuiusque proprium esse ‘ignem’ quo punitur; ait enim: “Ambulate in lumine ignis vestri et in flamma, quam accendistis vobismet ipsis”. Per quos sermones hoc videtur indicari, quod unusquisque peccatorum “flammam-” sibi ipse proprii ‘ignis’ ‘accendat”, et non in aliquem ignem, qui antea lam fuerit accensus ab alio vel ante ipsum substiterit, demergatur. Cuius ignis esca atque materia sunt nostra peccata, quae ab apostolo Paulo ‘ligna et faenum et stipula- nominantur. Et arbitror quod sicut in corpore escae abundantia et qualitas vel quantitas cibi contraria febres generat, et febres diversi vel modi vel temporis secundum eam mensuram, qua intemperies collecta materiam suggesserit ac fomitem febrium (quae materiae qualitas, ex diversa intemperie congregata, causa vel acerbioris morbi vel prolixioris existit): ita anima cum multitudinem malorum operum et abundantiam in se congregaverit peccatorum, conpetenti tempore omnis illa malorum congregatio effervescit ad supplicium atque inflammatur ad poenas; cum etiam mens ipsa vel conscientia per divinam virtutem omnia in memorlam recipiens, quorum in semet signa quaedam ac formas, cum peccaret, expresserat, et singulorum, quae vel foede ac turpiter gesserat vel etiam impie commiserat, historiam quandam scelerum suorum ante oculos videbit expositam: tunc et ipsa conscientia propriis stimulis agitatur atque conpungitur et sui ipsa efficitur accusatrix et testis. Quod ita sensisse etiam Paulum apostolum puto cum dicit: “Inter se invicem cogitationibus aceusantibus aut etiam defendentibus in die, quo iudicabit deus oceulta hominum secundum evangelium meum per lesum Christum”. Ex quo intellegitur quod cirea ipsam animae substantiam tormenta quaedam ex ipsis peecatorum noxiis affectibus generantur. 5. Et ne satis tibi difficilis huius rei intellectus appareat, considerari possibile est ex his passionum vitis, quae animabus accidere solent, id est cum vel flammis amoris exuritur anima vel zeli aut livoris ignibus maceratur, aut cum irae agitatur insania vel tristitiae inmensitate consumitur, quomodo horum malorum nimietates aliquanti intolerabiliter ferentes, mortem subire quam huiuscemodi cruciatus perpeti tolerabilius habuere. Requires sane si his, qui vitiorum malis istis, quae supra diximus, inretiti sunt nec emendationis aliquid in hac vita adhue positi comparare sibimet potuerunt et ita ex hoc mundo abscesserunt, sufficiat illis ad poenam quod illis ipsis perdurantibus in se noxus affectibus eruciantur, id est irae vel furoris vel insaniae vel maeroris, quorum utique mortiferum virus nullo in hae vita emendationis medicamento mitigatum est; an his affectibus immutatis generalis poenae stimulis vexabuntur. Sed et aliam suppliciorum speciem intellegi arbitror posse, quia sicut quidem sentimus soluta corporis membra atque a suis invicem divulsa conpagibus inmensi doloris generare cruciatum, ita cum anima extra ordinem atque conpagem vel eam harmoniam, qua ad bene agendum et utihter sentiendum a deo creata est, fuerit inventa nec sibimet ipsi rationabilium motuum conpagine consonare, poenam cruciatumque putanda sit suimet ipsius ferre discidnu, et inconstantiae suae atque inordinationis sentire supplicium. Quae animae dissolutio atque divulsio cum adhibiti ignis ratione fuerit explorata, sine dubio ad firmiorem sui eonpagem instaurationemque solidatur. 6. Multa sunt etiam alia quae nos latent, quae illi soli cognita sunt, qui est medicus animarum nostrarum. Si enim ad corporis sanitatem pro his vitus, quae per escam potumque collegimus, necessariam habemus interdum austerioris ac mordacioris medicamenti curam, nonnumquam vero, si id viti qualitas depoposcerit, rigore ferri et sectionis asperitate indigemus, quodsi et haec supergressus fuerit morbi modus, ad ultimum conceptum vitium etiam ignis exurit:
pass_a_gloss: But because our discussion has reminded us of the future judgment and of the repayment and punishments of sins, according to what the holy scriptures and ecclesiastical preaching threaten, because in the time of judgment 'eternal fire' and 'outer darkness' and 'prison' and 'furnace' and other things similar to these have been prepared for sinners, let us see what ought to be thought about these things. But in order that we may come to these things in a suitable order, it seems to me that the discussion of the resurrection must first be undertaken, so that we may know what it is that comes either to punishment or to rest and beatitude; about which we have also discussed more fully in other books, which we have written about the resurrection, and have shown what seems to us about this. But also now, because of the sequence of the treatise, it does not seem absurd to repeat a few things from that, especially because some people are offended in the ecclesiastical faith, because we seem to believe foolishly and utterly without wisdom about the resurrection, especially heretics, to whom I think we must respond in this way. If they confess that there is a resurrection of the dead, let them answer us: what is it that has died, is it not the body? Therefore, the resurrection of the body will occur.

bible_refs.note: Paul's description of the spiritual body

pass_b_english: Our discussion has reminded us of the coming judgment, the repayment for sin, and the punishments that await sinners, just as the holy Scriptures threaten and ecclesiastical preaching declares. For at the time of judgment, 'eternal fire' and 'outer darkness' and 'prison' and 'furnace' and other things like these have been prepared for sinners, so let us consider what we ought to think about these matters. But to approach them in proper order, it seems to me we must first take up the question of the resurrection, so that we may know what it is that comes either to punishment or to rest and blessedness. We have discussed this more fully in other books written on the resurrection, where we set out what seemed right to us. Yet because of the flow of this treatise, it is not out of place to repeat a few points here, especially since some take offense at the church's faith, supposing that we believe foolishly and utterly unwisely about the resurrection—above all heretics, to whom I think we must respond in this way. If they themselves confess that there is a resurrection of the dead, let them answer us: what is it that has died, if not the body? Therefore a resurrection of the body will take place.

Then let them say whether they think we are to have use of bodies or not. I think that when the apostle Paul says, 'It is sown a physical body, it is raised a spiritual body' (1 Corinthians 15:42-44), they cannot deny that a body rises or that in the resurrection we shall have use of bodies. So then, if it is certain that we must have use of bodies, and those bodies that have fallen are proclaimed to 'rise' (for nothing is properly said to rise except what has fallen before), there is no doubt that they rise so that we may be clothed with them again after the resurrection. One thing follows from the other. For if bodies rise, they rise without doubt for our clothing, and if we must exist in bodies (as we certainly must), we ought to exist in none other than our own bodies. If it is true that bodies rise and spiritual bodies rise, there can be no doubt that they are said to rise from the dead with corruption cast off and mortality laid aside; otherwise it would be vain and superfluous to rise from the dead only to die again. This can be understood even more clearly if anyone carefully considers what the quality of a 'physical body' is, which, sown in the earth, recovers the quality of a 'spiritual body.' For from the 'physical body' the very power of the resurrection and grace bring forth a 'spiritual body,' when it is transformed from 'dishonor' into 'glory.'

Since, then, the heretics consider themselves most learned and most wise, let us question them: does every body have some schema, that is, is every body shaped by some condition? If they say there is a body that is not shaped by any condition, they will appear the most ignorant and most foolish of all. No one will deny this unless they are completely alien to all learning. But if, following what is logical, they say that every body is certainly shaped by some condition, we will ask them whether they can demonstrate and describe for us the condition of a 'spiritual body'—which they certainly cannot do in any way. We will also ask them about the differences among those who rise. How will they show to be true what has been said: 'All flesh is not the same flesh, but there is one flesh of birds, another of fish; and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one, and the glory of the earthly is another; there is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead'? According to this reasoning, let them show us the differences of glory among heavenly bodies of those who rise. And if they attempt in any way to devise a rationale based on the differences of heavenly bodies, we will ask them to assign the differences of the resurrection also by comparison with earthly bodies. We understand that the apostle, wishing to describe how great the difference would be among those who rise 'in glory,' that is, the saints, took the comparison of heavenly bodies, saying: 'There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars.' And again, wishing to teach the differences of those who come to the resurrection unpurged in this life, that is, sinners, he takes an example from earthly things, saying: 'All flesh is not the same flesh, but there is one flesh of birds, another of fish.' Fittingly, heavenly things are compared to the saints, earthly things to sinners. These things have been said against those who deny 'the resurrection of the dead,' that is, the resurrection of bodies.

Now we turn our discussion to some of our own people who, whether from poverty of understanding or lack of explanation, introduce a very base and abject view of the resurrection of the body. We ask them how they understand a 'physical body' to be changed by the grace of the resurrection into a 'spiritual' one, and how they think that what is 'sown in weakness' will rise 'in power,' and what is 'sown in dishonor,' how it will rise 'in glory,' and what is 'sown in corruption,' how it will be transferred to 'incorruption.' Certainly if they believe the apostle that the body rising 'in glory and in power and in incorruptibility' has become 'spiritual,' it seems absurd and contrary to the apostle's meaning to say that it is again entangled in the passions of 'flesh and blood,' since the apostle plainly says: 'Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption.' And how do they take what the apostle says, that 'we shall all be changed'? This change is to be awaited according to that order which we set out above, in which we fittingly may hope for something worthy from divine grace. We believe this will happen in the order the apostle describes, when a 'bare grain of wheat or of some other grain' is sown in the earth, to which 'God gives a body as he chose,' after the 'grain' of 'wheat' itself has 'died.' So also our bodies must be thought of as 'grain' falling into the earth, in which the indwelling principle that contains the bodily substance, though the bodies have died and been corrupted and scattered, is nonetheless raised up by the word of God—that same principle which is always preserved in the substance of the body—and restored and repaired, just as the power that exists in a grain of wheat, after its corruption and death, repairs and restores the grain into the body of the stalk and the ear. And so for those who will deserve to obtain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, that principle of repairing the body, of which we spoke above, by God's command repairs a 'spiritual body' from an earthly and 'physical body,' one that can dwell in the heavens. But for those of lesser merit, or more abject, or even the last and most obscure, the glory and dignity of the body will be given according to the worth of each one's life and soul. Yet even for those destined for 'eternal fire' or for 'punishments,' by the very exchange of the resurrection the body that rises is so incorruptible that it cannot be corrupted or dissolved even by punishments.

If, therefore, the quality of the body that will rise from the dead is such, let us now see what the threat of 'eternal fire' means. For we find in the prophet Isaiah that it is designated as each one's own 'fire' by which he is punished; for he says: 'Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame you have kindled for yourselves.' By these words it seems to be indicated that each sinner 'kindles' his own proper 'flame' of 'fire,' and is not plunged into some fire that was lit before by another or that existed before him. The fuel and material of this fire are our sins, which the apostle Paul calls 'wood, hay, and straw.' I think that just as in the body the abundance and quality or quantity of food contrary to health generates fevers, and fevers of various kinds or durations according to the measure that the distemper, gathered from that material, has suggested and kindled the stimulus of fevers (which material quality, gathered from diverse distemper, is the cause of a more severe or more prolonged illness): so the soul, when it has gathered into itself the multitude of evil works and abundance of sins, at the fitting time all that gathering of evils boils up into punishment and is inflamed into penalties. Even the mind itself or conscience, by divine power receiving all things into memory of which, while sinning, it had impressed certain signs and forms upon itself, and seeing the history of its own crimes set before its eyes—each thing it had done foully and shamefully or even impiously—then that very conscience is stirred by its own goads and pricked, and itself becomes accuser and witness. I think the apostle Paul also understood this when he says: 'Their conflicting thoughts accusing or even excusing them on the day when God judges the secrets of men according to my gospel through Jesus Christ.' From this it is understood that certain torments are generated around the very substance of the soul from the harmful passions of sins themselves.

And lest the understanding of this matter seem too difficult to you, it can be considered from those passions of life which commonly befall souls: that is, when the soul is burned with flames of love, or consumed by fires of zeal or envy, or when it is agitated by the madness of anger or consumed by the immensity of sadness. How some, intolerably bearing the excesses of these evils, have found it more tolerable to undergo death than to endure such torments. One may reasonably ask whether for those who are caught in those evils of vice which we spoke of above, and have not been able to procure any amendment for themselves in this life, and so have departed from this world, it suffices for punishment that they be tortured by those same harmful passions enduring in them—that is, anger or fury or madness or grief—whose deadly poison has been mitigated by no medicine of amendment in this life; or whether, with those passions changed, they will be vexed by the general stimuli of punishment. And I think another species of punishment can be understood: for just as we feel that the loosening of the body's members and their separation from their mutual joints generates the torment of immense pain, so when the soul is found outside the order and structure or that harmony by which it was created by God for doing well and feeling rightly, and it does not harmonize with itself in the structure of rational movements, the punishment and torment of bearing its own division, and of feeling the penalty of its own inconstancy and disorder, must be reckoned. Which dissolution and tearing of the soul, when explored by reason of the applied fire, will without doubt be solidified into a firmer restoration of its own structure.
